a: The words of Agur son of Jakeh
p: Agur and his father Jakeh appear nowhere else in the Bible. He may have been a sage from outside Israel.
b: Nothing else is known of Agur ('agur, perhaps "gathered" or "hired") or of Jakeh. The heading does not call him a king or an Israelite, and if "the oracle" is really the place name Massa (see the next note), he came from an Arab tribe descended from Ishmael. The book had already said that wisdom was found among "the peoples of the east" (1 Kings 4:30), and Job is set in the same world. Jewish tradition made Agur a pen name for Solomon: Kohelet Rabbah 1:1 lists Agur, Jakeh, Ithiel and Lemuel among Solomon's names, and Rashi explains Agur as the one who "gathered" understanding. Most modern scholars take the heading at its word: these are the words of another, otherwise unknown wise man, added near the end of the book.

a: the oracle
p: Massa' means a weighty message, an oracle. It is also the name of an Arab tribe, and many read "Agur of Massa".
b: Massa' comes from the verb "lift, carry": a burden, and so a solemn message from God, as in "the oracle about Babylon" (Isaiah 13:1). But Massa was also a son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30), a people of north Arabia, and 31:1 again has the word right after "king". So many scholars read "Agur son of Jakeh, of Massa" and "Lemuel, king of Massa", making both men Arabian sages. The difficulty here is the article: the Hebrew says hammassa', "the massa'", which suits "the oracle" better than a tribe, unless one changes it slightly to hammassa'i, "the Massaite". The Plain follows the Hebrew as it stands. Either way, the word gives Agur's sayings the weight of a prophet's message.

a: So says the man
p: Ne'um haggever, "the declaration of the man", here "So says the man", is the way Balaam and David introduce inspired words.
b: Ne'um is the word of the prophets' "declares the LORD". With haggever, "the man", it appears only in Balaam's last two poems (Numbers 24:3, 15) and David's last words: "The declaration of David son of Jesse, / the declaration of the man set up on high" (2 Samuel 23:1). So Agur's sayings are framed with two prophetic words, "oracle" and "declaration". Yet what follows begins with a confession that the speaker knows nothing (30:2–3). Some readers see deliberate irony: the man whose words are announced like an oracle has no knowledge of his own, only what God's word gives (30:5).

a: I am more beast than man
p: Ba'ar is the stupidity of a farm animal. Agur says he is not even fully human in understanding.
b: Ba'ar is the dullness of cattle, the word of a psalmist who says, "I was a dumb animal with you" (Psalm 73:22). Me'ish can mean "more than any man" or "less than a man". Readers take the confession three ways. Some hear real humility: the sage admits that human wisdom cannot reach God (compare Job 28). Others hear sarcasm aimed at teachers who claim to know God's ways. Others again, from the Greek on, read it as a lead-in to trust in God's word (30:5). The Talmud has Solomon say it in repentance after his mother's rebuke (Bavli Sanhedrin 70b, on 31:1–2), reading me'ish as "more than the man", Noah, "a man of the ground" (Genesis 9:20) who drank too much.

a: knowledge of the Holy One
t: The Holy One, or holy ones?
p: Qedoshim is plural. It is a way of naming God, as in 9:10, though some take it as "the holy ones".
b: The Hebrew says "knowledge of holy ones". Most take the plural as a title of God, like Elohim, and 9:10 pairs the same word with "the fear of the LORD" (see the note there). Others read "the holy ones", the angels of God's council (Job 5:1; Psalm 89:5–7), whose knowledge Agur lacks. The negative of the first line ("I have not learned") probably carries into the second, as the Plain has it, though the Hebrew verb is positive, "I know". Some read it as a contrast: "yet I know the knowledge of the Holy One". The Greek takes that road (see the variant).

a: Who has climbed up to heaven and come back down?
t: Who has gone up to heaven?
p: Agur's question echoes Deuteronomy, and Paul and John answer it with Christ.
b: Deuteronomy says God's command is near: "It is not in the sky, so that you would ask, 'Who will climb up into the sky for us and get it, and tell it to us so we can do it?'" (Deuteronomy 30:12). Agur's question is the same: no human has gone up to learn heaven's secrets. Baruch, a deuterocanonical book, asks it of Wisdom: "Who went up into heaven and took her, and brought her down from the clouds?" (Baruch 3:29). The New Testament gives the question a new answer. Paul reads Deuteronomy's words of Christ: "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will climb up into heaven?' (that is, to bring Christ down)" (Romans 10:6). In John, Jesus says, "Nobody has gone up into heaven except the one who came down out of heaven, the Son of Man" (John 3:13), which many readers take as an answer to Agur.

a: Who has collected the wind in his two fists?
t: Wind in a fist, water in a robe
p: Agur asks six questions. The first four picture the Creator holding wind, water and earth as easily as a person holds a coat.
b: Agur asks six questions: four begin "Who" and two begin "What". The four "Who" questions climb from sky to earth. Chofnayim are the two fists or cupped hands, a double handful. Bundling water in a robe pictures the clouds holding rain, as in Job: "He bundles water up inside his clouds, / and the cloud does not split beneath it" (Job 26:8). Setting up the ends of the earth is founding the world on its pillars (Job 38:4–6; Psalm 104:5). Isaiah asks the same kind of question: who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand (Isaiah 40:12)? The answer to each is God. The questions are rhetorical, and Job 38–41 is the Bible's longest example of the form. The Greek has "in his bosom" for the hands.

a: What is his name, and what is his son's name?
p: God, Israel, a human expert, or the Son of God? The question has been read in all these ways.
b: God and Israel. Many take the one who rules wind and water to be God, and his "son" to be Israel, called "my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22), or the king, God's son (Psalm 2:7). Waltke and Van Leeuwen read the first questions as about God. A sarcastic challenge. Toy, Whybray and Longman hear a taunt: name the human being who has done this, and his family, if you can. Rashi answers "Moses", who went up the mountain, and asks for his descendants. The divine council. The Greek says "his children", and Franklyn reads the sons of God, the heavenly beings. The Son. Augustine (Letter 102) applied the verse to Christ, and Matthew Henry saw the Messiah's name "as yet secret". Many Christian readers today read it this way in light of John 3:13, while others warn against using it as proof of the Trinity.

a: You must know!
p: Ki teda' is the same jab God uses in Job 38:5, and the Plain renders it the same way there and here: "You must know!"
b: Ki teda' can mean "for you know", "surely you know" or "if you know". God uses the same words to Job: "Who decided its size? You must know!" (Job 38:5). There it is plainly ironic, and many hear the same irony here: no one can answer. Others hear an invitation: the reader does know, because the next verse gives the answer in God's word. The Greek turns it into a purpose clause, ἵνα γνῷς, "so that you may know". Rahlfs prints it, with Codices Alexandrinus and Ephraemi. Swete's notes show that Codex Vaticanus lacks it.

a: Every saying of God is refined like metal.
p: Agur quotes a psalm found twice in the Bible, Psalm 18:30 and 2 Samuel 22:31, changing "the LORD" to "God".
b: The psalm reads: "The LORD's word is refined like metal. / He is a shield for everyone who takes shelter in him" (Psalm 18:30; also 2 Samuel 22:31). Agur's version names God as Eloah, the word Job's poetry uses, and adds "every". The verb tsaraf is a metalworker's word for silver smelted until the impurities are gone, as in "silver smelted in a crucible in the ground, / refined seven times" (Psalm 12:6). After confessing that he has no wisdom of his own (30:2–3), Agur points to the one thing that can be trusted: what God has said. This is one of the clearest places where Proverbs, a book of human observation, leans on revealed Scripture.

a: Add nothing to his words
t: Do not add to God's words
p: The warning repeats Deuteronomy and is echoed at the end of the Bible, in Revelation 22:18.
b: Moses told Israel: "Do not add anything to the word I am commanding you, and do not take anything away from it" (Deuteronomy 4:2; compare Deuteronomy 12:32). Revelation ends with the same warning: "If anyone adds anything to them, God will add to that person the plagues written in this book" (Revelation 22:18). Since 30:5 quotes a psalm and 30:6 echoes Deuteronomy, many scholars think Agur, or the editor who placed him here, already knew a body of written Scripture and wanted to keep human sayings below it. The one who adds will be "shown up as a liar": his additions will be exposed as his own words, not God's.

a: Two things I ask from you.
p: Agur turns from speaking about God to speaking to him, and he asks for just enough.
b: This is the only prayer in the book. It is also the first numerical saying in the chapter ("two things"), and it sets the tone for the rest: honesty and contentment. "Before I die" means "for the rest of my life". The first request is moral (keep me from lies), the second is about money (give me neither too little nor too much), and 30:9 explains the second: both wealth and poverty tempt a person away from God.

a: Feed me with the bread that is my share
p: Lechem chuqqi is bread measured out, like the manna each day, and it anticipates the Lord's Prayer.
b: Choq is a set amount, a ration (31:15 uses it of the share given to servants). The manna came the same way: "The people are to go out and pick up each day's share on its own day" (Exodus 16:4). Jesus taught his followers to pray, "Give us today our bread for the coming day" (Matthew 6:11), and Paul says, "if we have food and something to wear, that will be enough for us" (1 Timothy 6:8). Agur does not praise poverty. He asks for enough, because enough keeps a person close to God.

a: Who is the LORD?
p: The full man forgets God, as Moses warned and as Pharaoh boasted.
b: Pharaoh's question was, "Who is this LORD, that I should heed his voice?" (Exodus 5:2). Moses warned Israel that plenty breeds the same spirit: "You will eat and be full... Then do not let your heart grow proud, so that you forget the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 8:12–14). Agur fears that in himself. The name used is YHWH, "the LORD", the only time Agur uses the divine name; Proverbs as a whole uses it often.

a: lay my hands on the name of my God
p: Tafas means "grab, seize". The thief who gets caught may swear falsely by God's name to clear himself.
b: Tafas means to seize or take hold of. The phrase is unusual. Many think it means to abuse God's name by a false oath: a poor man steals, and when accused swears by God that he is innocent. The law links the two sins: "he may find something lost and deny it. He may swear falsely" (Leviticus 6:3), and "Do not swear by my name to a lie" (Leviticus 19:12). The Greek supports this ("I steal and swear by the name of God"), and so does Jerome's Latin, peierem nomen Dei mei, "I swear falsely by the name of my God". Others take it more broadly: theft by one of God's people drags his name into disgrace. Either way, poverty tempts to sin against neighbor and God at once.

a: Do not run down a servant to his master
p: Lashan is to slander with the tongue. Eved here is a household servant or slave.
b: Lashan, from lashon, "tongue", means to slander or inform on. 'Eved covers both a hired servant and a slave; the Plain has "servant", since the setting is a household. The servant has no power to answer back, but he can curse, and the curse of the wronged was believed to land (compare 26:2). The saying fits Deuteronomy's protection of the powerless: "Do not hand a slave over to his master when he has escaped from his master to you" (Deuteronomy 23:15). The Greek reads this verse in just that way (see the variant). The Hebrew text has the plural "masters" (the Qere), a plural of majesty for one master.

a: There is a generation
p: Dor means a generation, but also a kind or class of people. Four lines begin with it.
b: Dor usually means the people living at one time, but it can mean a kind of people, a crowd who share a character (Psalm 14:5 has bedor tsaddiq, which the Plain of Psalms renders "the circle of the righteous"; compare Psalm 24:6). Four sayings in a row begin with the word, building a portrait of one type: they curse parents, think themselves clean, look down on others and devour the poor. The first offense was capital in Israel's law: "Anyone who curses his father or his mother must be put to death" (Exodus 21:17). The list has no number, but it works like the numbered lists that follow. The Greek begins each line with "an evil offspring".

a: washed of its own filth
p: Tso'ah is excrement, a deliberately coarse word for moral filth.
b: Tso'ah is human excrement (Deuteronomy 23:13 uses a related word; Isaiah 4:4 speaks of the LORD washing away "the filth of the daughters of Zion"). The saying is blunt on purpose: people who think themselves spotless are covered in dirt they cannot see. Jesus spoke the same way of those who clean the outside of the cup (Matthew 23:25–28).

a: whose teeth are swords
p: The greedy are pictured as beasts that eat the poor alive.
b: The last portrait is a predator. Metall'ot are the big jaw teeth, and ma'akhalot are butchers' knives. A psalmist describes his enemies the same way: "Their teeth are spears and arrows; / their tongue is a sharp sword" (Psalm 57:4). The prophets accuse Israel's rich of eating the poor (Micah 3:2–3; Amos 8:4). The poor ('aniyyim) and needy ('evyonim) return at the end of Lemuel's words (31:9) and in the woman of strength's open hand (31:20), so the last chapters of Proverbs keep coming back to them.

a: The leech has two daughters
p: 'Aluqah, found only here, is the blood-sucking leech. Her two daughters are her cries, "Give! Give!"
b: 'Aluqah appears only here; the related Arabic and Aramaic words name the leech. Her "two daughters" may be her two suckers, or simply her offspring, who have only one word between them. Many scholars think this line was once a separate riddle placed in front of the numerical saying, since it counts two, not three and four. The Greek makes the numbers match: "The leech had three daughters, dearly loved, and these three did not satisfy her", with a fourth that was never content.

a: Here are three that are never full
p: This is a numerical saying, a form used in Israel, Ugarit and Aram: name a number, then one more.
b: The pattern "three... four" (x, then x + 1) is a way of saying "several, and here is the one that matters most". The list that follows has four items, and the last one usually carries the weight. Proverbs uses it in 6:16–19 ("six... seven") and four times in this chapter (30:15–16, 18–19, 21–23, 29–31); 30:24–28 has the plain number four. Amos opens with "for three crimes... and for four" (Amos 1:3), Job with "Through six troubles he will save you, / and in seven" (Job 5:19). The form is older than Israel. A Ugaritic poem says Baal hates two kinds of feasts, three the Rider of the Clouds (KTU 1.4 iii 17–21), and the Aramaic Story of Ahiqar has "two things are good, and a third is pleasing to Shamash".

a: Sheol, and the closed-up womb
p: The list pairs the grave, which always wants more dead, with the womb that longs for life.
b: Sheol, the world of the dead, is never full (27:20; Habakkuk 2:5). Beside it stands the "closed-up womb" ('otser rachem), a woman who cannot conceive and longs for a child, as Rachel cried, "Give me children! If you don't, I am a dead woman" (Genesis 30:1). Then come dry land that drinks up any rain and fire that consumes any fuel. Death and birth, earth and fire: the four cover the whole world, and none of them can be satisfied. The leech's "Give! Give!" (30:15) is the voice of all four. The Greek reads the second item as "a woman's passion" (see the variant).

a: The eye that makes fun of a father
p: The child who mocks his parents will die without burial, his body left for the birds.
b: The punishment is the worst death an Israelite could imagine: to lie unburied, food for birds. The covenant curse warned, "Your corpses will feed every bird that flies and every wild animal" (Deuteronomy 28:26), and prophets threatened kings with it (1 Kings 14:11; Jeremiah 22:19). The eye that sneered is the part that is lost. The command to honor parents comes with a promise of long life (Exodus 20:12), and this saying is its dark mirror. Nesher, "eagle", includes the griffon vulture, which fits a scavenger here (compare Micah 1:16).

a: Three things are a wonder beyond me
p: An eagle, a snake, a ship and a man with a woman. Readers disagree about what joins them.
b: They leave no trace. No track is left in the sky, on rock or in water, and so (30:20) the adulterous woman leaves no evidence; this is the older and still common reading (Toy, McKane). Movement that cannot be explained. Each moves with ease through a medium that seems unable to carry it, and the last is the mystery of attraction and love between a man and a woman, which the sage admires, not condemns (Fox, Van Leeuwen; compare Song of Songs 8:6–7). On this view 30:20 is a separate saying, hooked on by the word "way", that contrasts love's wonder with cold adultery. Mastery. Some see a strong creature in control of each element. The verb nifle'u, "are a wonder beyond", comes from the root of Psalm 139:6, "Knowing like this is a wonder beyond me", and Psalm 139:14 uses it of God's works: "Your works are wonders". The Hebrew text writes the number "four" in 30:18 as arba' and reads it as arba'ah (Ketiv and Qere), with no change in meaning.
r: 30:20; Psalm 139:6; Psalm 139:14; Song of Songs 8:6–7; Job 42:3

a: with a young woman
p: 'Almah is the word of Isaiah 7:14. Here it plainly means a young woman in a sexual relationship.
b: 'Almah is a young woman old enough to marry. It is the word in Isaiah 7:14, which the Greek there rendered parthenos, "virgin", and Matthew 1:23 quotes in that form. Readers on both sides of the debate over Isaiah 7:14 cite this verse. Those who say 'almah does not by itself mean "virgin" point out that "the way of a man with a young woman" is most naturally sexual. Others reply that the sexual sense lies in the phrase, not the word, and that the girl may have been a virgin until then. The Greek of Proverbs does not have "young woman" at all here (see the variant).
r: Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23; Genesis 24:43; Exodus 2:8; Song of Songs 6:8

a: She eats and wipes her mouth clean
t: Eating as a picture of sex
p: The adulterous woman "eats", wipes her mouth, and feels no guilt, as if she had only had a meal.
b: Eating is a common picture of sex in Proverbs and the Song of Songs: Folly invites, "Water you steal tastes sweet, / and bread from hiding places is a delight" (9:17), and the bride invites her lover to eat (Song of Songs 4:16). Here the woman treats adultery like a snack and, mouth wiped, says she did no wrong. The point is not her sex but her lack of conscience, and it matches the earlier warnings about the "strange woman", of whom 2:17 says, "the covenant of her God has slipped from her mind" (see also 7:10–23). Modern readers ask why the warning names a woman only; the book is addressed to young men, and its warnings speak to their temptations (5:15–20).

a: The earth quakes beneath three things
p: Four people who rise out of their place: a slave made king, a fool well fed, an unloved wife, a maid in charge.
b: The earth shakes under weight it cannot bear. The slave who becomes king and the fool who is full appear elsewhere as things "not fitting" (19:10; Ecclesiastes 10:5–7). The unloved woman recalls Leah: "The LORD saw that Leah was the unloved one" (Genesis 29:31). The slave woman taking her mistress's place recalls Hagar: "When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress became small in her eyes" (Genesis 16:4). Egyptian texts such as the Admonitions of Ipuwer describe social chaos the same way, with slaves ruling their masters. Readers differ on the tone. Many take it as a serious defense of order. Others hear humor: the sage laughs at upstarts who cannot handle their new position. Modern readers note that the saying looks at the world from the side of masters and mistresses.

a: Four are among the small things of the earth
p: Ants, hyraxes, locusts and lizards: weak creatures that thrive by wisdom, not strength.
b: Solomon "talked about beasts and birds, about creatures that creep, and about fish" (1 Kings 4:33), and sayings drawn from animals were part of wisdom across the ancient Near East. Each of the four has no power, and each succeeds anyway: ants by planning ahead (compare 6:6–8), hyraxes by choosing a safe home, locusts by moving together without a ruler, the lizard by slipping into palaces. The phrase chakhamim mechukkamim is literally "wise, made wise", and the Plain has "schooled in wisdom". The Greek says "wiser than the wise". Calling animals "a people" ('am) gives them a kind of nationhood, which makes the lesson for Israel and its readers plainer.

a: The rock badgers
p: Shefannim are rock hyraxes, small furry animals that live in cliffs in Israel. The KJV calls them conies.
b: The rock hyrax (Procavia capensis) looks like a large guinea pig and lives in colonies among rocks, as at En Gedi by the Dead Sea. "The cliffs are where the rock badgers hide" (Psalm 104:18). They were unclean food because they seemed to chew the cud but had no split hoof (Leviticus 11:5). The KJV's "conies" (rabbits) was a guess. The name "rock badger" is old but zoologically wrong; hyraxes are not badgers.

a: but out they go in rows, every one of them
p: Chotsets means "dividing": the swarm moves in divisions like an army with no general.
b: Chotsets comes from a root meaning to divide, so "in companies". Joel describes a locust plague as an army that "does not break ranks" (Joel 2:7–8). The point is order without a king, which is wisdom of a kind. The Greek adds that they march "at one command, in good order".

a: The lizard can be held in two hands
p: Semamit is probably a gecko, which clings to walls. The KJV has "spider".
b: Semamit appears only here. Most scholars identify it as the house gecko, which climbs walls on sticky toe pads and turns up inside the finest buildings. The Greek kalabōtēs is a spotted lizard. Jerome's Latin also has a lizard (stellio); the KJV has "spider". The Hebrew line can mean "you can catch it with your hands" or "it grips with its hands"; either way, a creature anyone could grab lives where kings live.

a: the rooster with its trim waist
t: A rooster, a greyhound, or a war horse?
p: Zarzir motnayim, "one girded at the waist", is unknown. Guesses include a rooster, a greyhound and a horse.
b: The phrase means something like "the girded of loins", a creature with a lean, tight waist. The Greek took it as a rooster ("a rooster walking proudly among hens"), Jerome's Latin as "a rooster girded at the loins" (gallus succinctus lumbos), and many modern versions follow. The KJV has "greyhound", and some propose a war horse or a starling, which is what zarzir means in later Hebrew. The Plain follows the rooster reading, with its uncertainty marked here. The last line is also unclear (see the next note).

a: a king with his troops beside him
p: The rare word 'alqum may mean "his people, his army", or be two words: "no rising up" against him.
b: 'Alqum occurs only here. Many relate it to the Arabic al-qawm, "the people", and read "a king with his army" or "with his people around him". The KJV took it as 'al qum, "no rising up": "a king against whom there is no rising up". Others emend the text. Jerome's Latin agrees with the KJV: "nor is there a king who can resist him". The Greek has "a king making a speech before a nation". Whatever the exact sense, the saying ends where Agur's sayings began, with human power, and the next verse warns against exalting oneself.

a: If you have played the godless fool by lifting yourself up
p: Nabal, the godless fool, becomes a verb here. The cure for pride and scheming is to stop talking.
b: Navalta, "you have played the nabal", uses the verb of the godless fool (see 30:22). The scheming (zammota) is the bad sense of the planning word zamam. The remedy is a gesture: a hand on the mouth. Job makes it when God has spoken: "I lay a hand across my mouth" (Job 40:4), and Micah says the nations will put their hands on their mouths in shame (Micah 7:16). After Agur's opening confession (30:2–3), his words end the same way: silence before God and before others.

a: squeezing the nose brings out blood
p: The Hebrew plays on 'af, which means both "nose" and "anger". The same verb, "squeeze", runs through all three lines.
b: Mits, "squeezing" or "churning", appears three times: milk churned in a skin bag gives curds, a squeezed nose bleeds, and "squeezed" anger gives a quarrel. The wordplay is that 'af is "nose", and its dual 'appayim, "two nostrils", is the usual word for anger (the snorting nose of a furious person). So the third line is literally "squeezing of nostrils". English cannot carry the pun. The point is cause and effect: pressing on anger always produces a fight (compare 15:1; 17:14). The Greek reads, "if you draw out words, judgments and fights will come".

a: The words of Lemuel, a king
p: Lemuel is unknown outside this chapter. Jewish tradition made him Solomon and his mother Bathsheba.
b: Lemu'el means "belonging to God" (compare Lael, Numbers 3:24). No king of Israel or Judah had the name, and 31:2–3 uses Aramaic words (bar "son", melakhin "kings"), so many scholars think he ruled a people east of Israel, perhaps Massa (see the variant). The rabbis identified him with Solomon. Kohelet Rabbah 1:1 counts Lemuel among Solomon's names. The Talmud says Bathsheba saw Solomon drinking, tied him to a pillar and scolded him with these words (Bavli Sanhedrin 70b). Numbers Rabbah 10:4 sets the scene on the night the Temple was finished, when Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter and slept late, delaying the morning offering, until his mother woke him. In Israel the king's mother was a power at court: "a throne was set out for the king's mother. She sat at his right" (1 Kings 2:19).

a: with which his mother disciplined him
p: Yasar, "discipline", is the verb of musar. This is the only teaching in Proverbs given in a mother's own words.
b: Yisserattu is from yasar, the verb behind musar, "discipline": instruction that includes correction (see the note at 1:2). The father's talks of chapters 1–9 tell the son, "do not walk away from your mother's teaching" (1:8; compare 6:20), but only here does a mother speak. Ancient instructions were nearly always from father to son: the Egyptian Ptahhotep and Amenemope, the Sumerian Shuruppak and the Aramaic Ahiqar all have a man teaching his son or pupil. A queen mother instructing a king has no close parallel. Many think the poem of the woman of strength that follows (31:10–31) is meant to be read with her words, a mother's picture of the wife she wants her son to find.

a: What, my son?
p: The threefold "what" is a cry of concern. Bar, "son", is Aramaic, not the usual Hebrew ben.
b: The Hebrew is clipped: "What, my son? What, son of my womb?" It may mean "What shall I say to you?" or "What are you doing?", or mah may be an exclamation, "Listen!". The repetition is emotional, a mother's appeal before she warns. "Son of my vows" suggests a son she prayed for and promised to God, as Hannah did: "if you... will give your servant a male child, then I will give him to the LORD for his whole life" (1 Samuel 1:11). The Aramaic bar (three times) instead of Hebrew ben is one of the signs that Lemuel came from outside Israel, or that the poem was written in a dialect touched by Aramaic.

a: Do not hand your strength over to women
p: The word for "strength" is chayil, the same word as the "woman of strength" in 31:10.
b: Chayil means strength, ability, wealth, even an army. The queen mother warns her son not to spend it on many women, the royal harem that ruined kings. Deuteronomy's law of the king says, "He must not take many wives for himself, or his heart will turn aside" (Deuteronomy 17:17), and of Solomon we read, "Seven hundred wives belonged to him... His wives bent his heart away" (1 Kings 11:3). The same word returns in 31:10 and 31:29. Read together, the chapter moves from "do not give your chayil to women" to "a woman of chayil, who can find one?". The answer to many women is one woman of strength. "What wipes out kings" (lamchot melakhin, with an Aramaic plural) is unusual Hebrew, and its exact sense is uncertain. The Greek has "do not give your wealth to women".

a: It is not for kings, Lemuel
p: A king who drinks forgets the law and fails the weak. The danger is to justice.
b: Here the name is spelled Lemo'el, a variant of Lemu'el in 31:1; it is the same king. In the ancient world the king was the final judge. Lemuel's mother does not argue that wine is evil but that a ruler's judgment must stay clear (31:5). The prophets condemn leaders who are champions at drinking while they let the guilty off for a bribe (Isaiah 5:22–23), and priests and prophets who reel from strong drink (Isaiah 28:7). Ecclesiastes contrasts a land whose princes feast in the morning with one whose princes eat for strength, not to get drunk (Ecclesiastes 10:16–17). Priests on duty were forbidden wine: "You and your sons are not to drink wine or beer when you go into the tent of meeting" (Leviticus 10:9).
r: 31:5; Isaiah 5:11–12; Isaiah 5:22–23; Isaiah 28:7; Ecclesiastes 10:16–17; Leviticus 10:9; Hosea 7:5

a: beer
p: Shekar was mostly beer brewed from grain. It was not distilled liquor, which did not yet exist.
b: Shekar is an alcoholic drink other than grape wine: mainly barley beer, the everyday drink of Egypt and Mesopotamia, and perhaps date or pomegranate wine. The Plain says "beer", as in 20:1. The traditional English "strong drink" (KJV) can mislead: distilling spirits was unknown in the biblical world. Wine (yayin) and shekar are often paired (Leviticus 10:9; Numbers 6:3; 1 Samuel 1:15). In 31:4 the Hebrew can be read two ways (see the variant).

a: forget what the law says
p: Mechuqqaq is "what has been decreed", the law a king is bound to uphold.
b: Mechuqqaq is from chaqaq, "engrave, decree", and means what has been written into law. The king who drinks forgets it and "changes the judgment" (yeshanneh din) of "all the sons of affliction", the poor who depend on a fair court. Deuteronomy wanted the king to keep a copy of the law beside him and read it all his life (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). The Greek has "so that they do not drink and forget wisdom".

a: Give beer to someone who is perishing
p: Is this mercy for the suffering, a dig at drink's low use, or both?
b: Mercy. The verse lets the dying and the grieving dull their pain. The Talmud reports that a condemned man on the way to execution was given "a grain of frankincense in a cup of wine" to numb him, citing this verse, and that the leading women of Jerusalem provided it (Bavli Sanhedrin 43a). Mark says that at the crucifixion "they kept trying to give him myrrh-flavored wine, but he would not accept it" (Mark 15:23). Contrast. Many commentators hear a sharper point: wine is for the hopeless, not for those who rule. Kings have work to do; let those who have nothing left drink and forget. Both. The saying sets drink in its place: a comfort for the broken, a danger for the powerful. It does not command drinking, and it is not a general rule for everyone.

a: Open your mouth for the one who cannot speak
t: The king's duty to the voiceless
p: The real work of a king is to speak for those who have no voice in court.
b: The mute ('illem) are those who cannot plead their own case. Ancient kings boasted of this duty: Hammurabi's laws say he ruled "so that the strong might not oppress the weak" and to give justice to the orphan and the widow. Israel's royal psalm prays, "May he give justice to the poor of the people, / save the children of the needy" (Psalm 72:4), and "he will rescue the needy who cry for help, / and the poor who have no one to help them" (Psalm 72:12). Jeremiah says that judging the cause of the poor and needy is what it means to know the LORD (Jeremiah 22:16). The mother's last words turn from what the king must not do to what he must.

a: all who are left to fade away
p: Bene chalof is rare: the dying, the destitute, or perhaps orphans who are left behind.
b: Bene chalof is literally "sons of passing away". Chalaf means to pass on or vanish, so most read "those who are perishing" or "the destitute", people who are slipping out of sight. Some take it as "those left behind", orphans, from the sense "to succeed someone". The KJV has "such as are appointed to destruction". The Greek rewrites the verse: "Open your mouth with a word of God, and judge all soundly."

a: A woman of strength
p: Chayil is strength, ability, wealth, valor. "Virtuous" and "noble" catch only part of it.
b: 'Eshet chayil is the female form of gibbor chayil or ish chayil, used of warriors ("you mighty fighter", Judges 6:12), capable officials (Exodus 18:21) and men of substance like Boaz, "a man of great worth" (Ruth 2:1). The KJV's "virtuous woman" made her mainly moral, and modern versions choose "noble", "capable" or "excellent". The Greek has gynaika andreian, "a courageous woman", and Jerome's Latin mulierem fortem, "a strong woman". In Jewish English she is often "a woman of valor". The Plain says "strength" because 31:3 and 31:29 use the same word chayil, and it keeps that English for chayil alone. The poem's other strength word, 'oz (31:17, 25), is rendered "might", so that a reader can tell the two apart. Proverbs uses the phrase once before: "A woman of strength is her husband's crown" (12:4).

a: who can find one?
p: Verses 10–31 are an acrostic: each verse begins with the next of the 22 letters of the Hebrew alphabet.
b: The letters, in order: 10 alef ('eshet), 11 bet (batach), 12 gimel (gemalathu), 13 dalet (dareshah), 14 he (hayetah), 15 waw (vattaqom), 16 zayin (zamemah), 17 chet (chagerah), 18 tet (ta'amah), 19 yod (yadeha), 20 kaf (kappah), 21 lamed (lo'), 22 mem (marvaddim), 23 nun (noda'), 24 samekh (sadin), 25 ayin ('oz), 26 pe (piha), 27 tsade (tsofiyyah), 28 qof (qamu), 29 resh (rabbot), 30 shin (sheqer), 31 tav (tenu). An alphabet poem says "from A to Z": the whole of something. Psalms 111 and 112, Psalm 119 and Lamentations 1–4 use the form too, and Psalm 112 praises the God-fearing man the way this poem praises the woman. The Greek, which reorders the end of Proverbs, loses the acrostic. It also puts 31:26 ("She opened her mouth...") before 31:25, so its lines would run pe before ayin. That is the order of Lamentations 2, 3 and 4, against the ayin-before-pe of Lamentations 1 and the Hebrew of this poem. Whether the translator's Hebrew had that order, or the Greek moved the lines, is not known. In the Hebrew, "who can find?" is a question about how rare she is, not a claim that she does not exist.
r: Psalm 111; Psalm 112; Psalm 119; Lamentations 1; Lamentations 2; Lamentations 3; Psalm 34

a: Her price is far beyond red coral
t: Worth more than red coral, like Wisdom
p: The same comparison was made of Wisdom herself, so the woman reflects Wisdom.
b: Peninim are probably red coral (Lamentations 4:7), though some say pearls; the KJV has "rubies". Proverbs has said the same of Wisdom: "She is worth more than red coral" (3:15; compare 8:11), and finding her is like finding treasure (3:13; 8:35; compare 18:22, "Find a wife and you have found something good"). Many scholars, such as Claudia Camp and Christine Yoder, conclude that the book ends with a portrait of Wisdom in the shape of a real woman: Lady Wisdom of chapters 1–9 built her house (9:1), and the woman of strength runs hers. Others stress that the poem describes an actual ideal wife. The two readings can stand together.

a: and he never runs short of plunder
p: Shalal is spoil taken in war. The poem praises her in the language of hero songs.
b: Shalal is booty taken from a defeated enemy (Judges 5:30; 1 Samuel 30:20). Here it means profit, but the war word is chosen on purpose. Al Wolters argued that the poem borrows the style of a heroic hymn, the kind sung of warriors: she has chayil (31:10), gets "plunder" (31:11), hands out "prey" to her household (31:15), straps on might (31:17), toughens her arms (31:17) and laughs at the future (31:25). Her battlefield is the household and the market. The Greek kept the image: "such a woman will not lack fine spoils".

a: She looks for wool and flax
p: Clothmaking was women's work and a real economy: clothing for the house and goods for sale.
b: Wool came from sheep, flax was grown for linen, and turning them into cloth took more hours than almost any other household task. Excavated Israelite houses are full of loom weights and spindle whorls. At the tabernacle, "every skilled woman spun with her own hands and brought what she had spun" (Exodus 35:25). The woman of the poem does it gladly ("in the delight of her palms") and on a scale that makes a profit (31:18, 24). Carol Meyers and others have shown how much of the family economy of ancient Israel was in women's hands.

a: She has become like a trader's ships
p: Like merchant ships, she brings in goods from far away: imported food for her household.
b: Israel was not a seafaring nation, but its people knew the Phoenician fleets. Solomon's "Tarshish ships" came "bringing gold and silver, ivory, monkeys and apes" (1 Kings 10:22). The woman trades beyond her village, buying what her own fields do not grow. The image suits a family of some wealth, with servants (31:15), land (31:16) and fine clothes (31:22): the poem portrays the mistress of a large household.

a: handing out food to her household
p: Teref usually means a lion's prey. Choq is a set share, for the maids either food or tasks.
b: Teref is the torn prey of a lion (Genesis 49:9; Psalm 104:21; Nahum 2:12), used here for food, another touch of the heroic style (see 31:11). Choq is an allotted portion, the word of Agur's "bread that is my share" (30:8). It can mean food for the serving girls or their work for the day; most take it as food, parallel to the first line. She rises before dawn, as the diligent do in contrast to the lazy one (6:9–11).

a: She sets her plans on a field and gets it
p: She plans, buys a field and plants a vineyard from her own earnings.
b: Zamemah is the good sense of zamam, "to plan" (compare mezimmah, "discretion", 1:4). Buying land was a major decision, usually a man's. Israel's law let daughters inherit land when there were no sons (Numbers 27:1–11), and documents from Elephantine in Egypt (400s BC) show Jewish women owning and trading houses. The poem shows a wife acting with her own resources, with her husband's full trust (31:11). The Hebrew text writes "he plants" (Ketiv, nata') but is read "she plants" (Qere); the written form is likely a shortened spelling, and the meaning is the same.

a: She binds up her waist with might
t: Might tied on like a belt
p: To gird the waist is to get ready for hard work or battle.
b: People tucked their long robes into a belt to run, fight or work, as Elijah "bound up his clothes at the waist and ran" (1 Kings 18:46) and God tells Job, "Get your belt tight, like a man" (Job 38:3). The woman ties on might itself ('oz), and toughens her arms (vatte'ammets, from the verb of "Be strong and bold" in Joshua 1:6). It is one of several lines that give her a warrior's posture (see 31:11).

a: She tastes that her trading is good
p: Ta'amah... ki tov, "she tastes that it is good", echoes Psalm 34:8.
b: Ta'am means to taste, and so to test and perceive. The psalm says, "Taste and see: the LORD is good!" (Psalm 34:8), with the same verb and the same "that... good". Psalm 34 is also an acrostic, and it too teaches the fear of the LORD (Psalm 34:11). Her lamp burning all night means hard work but also a household that does not fall into darkness; of the wicked Proverbs says, "the lamp of the wicked will go out" (13:9; 24:20; compare 20:20). The Hebrew text's spelling of "night" differs from the reading (Ketiv ballayil, Qere ballaylah), with no change in meaning.

a: Her hands reach out to the distaff
t: Distaff, spindle, and an open hand
p: Verses 19 and 20 mirror each other: the hands that spin are the hands that give.
b: Kishor appears only here; it is probably the distaff that holds raw fiber, or a spindle whorl. Pelekh is the spindle. The two verses are built as a mirror (a chiasm): "her hands"... "her palms" (31:19), then "her palm"... "her hands" (31:20), with the same verb shillechah, "reach out", in both. The hands that make cloth open to the poor. Her work is not only for her own house; its profit reaches the needy that Lemuel's mother told him to defend (31:9).

a: Fine linen and purple are what she wears
p: Shesh is fine Egyptian linen and argaman is purple wool, dyed with the costly murex shellfish.
b: Purple dye was made from murex snails, collected on the Phoenician coast and processed in huge quantities to color a little wool. It was the color of kings and of the tabernacle hangings (Exodus 26:1; Judges 8:26). Fine linen (shesh) came from Egypt. The poem shows a woman whose work has made her household rich, and she dresses accordingly. Later, the rich man of Jesus' parable, who wore purple and fine linen every day (Luke 16:19), is a warning; here the same cloth is the reward of honest work. Her bedcovers (marvaddim) appear also in 7:16, but there in the strange woman's house.

a: People know her husband at the gates
p: The town gate was court and council. Her husband sits with the elders, and his honor rests partly on her.
b: The gate was where elders heard cases and witnessed deals: "Boaz went up to the town gate and sat down there" (Ruth 4:1), and later "All the people at the gate and the elders said, 'We are witnesses'" (Ruth 4:11). This is the only verse that describes the husband's activity, and it sits in the middle of a poem about her. His reputation in public depends on her work at home and in trade. The poem ends at the gates too, where her own deeds praise her (31:31).

a: hands over belts to the traders
p: Kena'ani, "Canaanite", came to mean a merchant, because the Phoenicians were the great traders.
b: The Hebrew says she supplies sashes "to the Canaanite". The Phoenicians, coastal Canaanites, dominated trade, and kena'ani came to mean "trader" (Job 41:6; Isaiah 23:8; Zephaniah 1:11). The Greek kept the literal "to the Canaanites". Sadin is a linen wrap or undergarment (Judges 14:12–13). She is a producer selling to wholesale buyers.

a: on her tongue is the teaching of loyal love
t: Torat chesed: a teaching of loyal love
p: Torah here is a parent's teaching, and chesed is loyal love. Her words teach kindness that keeps faith.
b: In Proverbs, torah is the teaching a parent or a sage gives, so the Plain says "teaching" here, as it does at 1:8: "do not walk away from your mother's teaching". Chesed is loyal love, the faithful kindness of covenant and family. Torat chesed can mean "kind teaching" (the KJV's "law of kindness") or "teaching about loyal love". Either way, the woman who works with her hands also teaches with her mouth, like Wisdom, who calls out in the streets (1:20–21). The link with Ruth runs here too: Ruth's chesed is praised in Ruth 3:10, just before Boaz calls her a woman of worth. Christians who support women teaching sometimes point to this verse; others reply that it speaks of a mother's teaching in the home.

a: She keeps watch on how her household is going
p: The tsade line starts with tsofiyyah, "watching". Wolters argued it is a pun on the Greek sophia, "wisdom".
b: The tsade line opens with tsofiyyah, "(she is) watching over". It is a participle, the form hymns use to praise someone by what they do, but its ending is odd: the expected form would be tsofah, and -iyyah is unusual. With that ending the word sounds almost exactly like the Greek sophia, "wisdom". Al Wolters (1985) argued that the poet chose the odd form on purpose, so that the woman is named Wisdom in a pun. Others think a Greek pun in a Hebrew poem unlikely, or doubt the poem is late enough. Either way, the poem calls her watchful, and the line says she never eats the bread of laziness, the opposite of the lazy one of 6:6–11.

a: Her sons stand up and call her happy
p: Ishsher, "call happy", is the verb of ashrei. Leah and Mary are called happy in the same way.
b: Vay'ashruha is from the root of ashrei, "happy" (see the note at 3:13). When her son Asher was born, Leah said, "Happy me! For daughters will call me happy" (Genesis 30:13). Mary says, "from this time on, every generation will count me blessed" (Luke 1:48), with the Greek verb makarizō, "call happy, call blessed," which the Septuagint uses for Leah's words in Genesis 30:13, and Christian readers who see Mary in this poem point to the link. Children standing up was a mark of respect (Job 29:8). The husband's words follow in 31:29.

a: Many daughters have done strong things
p: 'Asu chayil, "have done strength", is the blessing the people gave Boaz, and Balaam's word for Israel's victory.
b: The phrase 'asah chayil means to act with strength or to do well. At Ruth's wedding, the people bless Boaz: "May you do worthy things in Ephrathah and make a name in Bethlehem" (Ruth 4:11). Balaam foresees a day when "Israel does mighty deeds" (Numbers 24:18). "Daughters" here means women in general. The husband's praise sets his wife above all women, much as the lover of the Song of Songs says that there are many queens, but his beloved is unique (Song of Songs 6:8–9).
orig: רַבּוֹת בָּנוֹת עָשׂוּ חָיִל (rabbot banot 'asu chayil)
r: Ruth 4:11; Numbers 24:18; Psalm 118:15; Song of Songs 6:8–9; 31:10

a: Charm is a lie, and beauty is a breath
p: Hevel, "breath, vapor", is Ecclesiastes' key word. Charm deceives and beauty does not last.
b: Chen, "charm, grace", can deceive, and yofi, "beauty", is hevel, a breath that is gone in a moment, the word Ecclesiastes uses for everything "under the sun". Proverbs has compared "a lovely woman who has turned her back on good sense" to a gold ring in a pig's snout (11:22). God told Samuel, "A human sees what is before the eyes, but the LORD sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). Peter tells Christian women that their beauty should not come from braided hair, gold or fine clothes, but from the hidden self within, a mild and calm spirit, which God counts precious (1 Peter 3:3–4). None of these says beauty is bad, only that it is not what lasts.
orig: שֶׁקֶר הַחֵן וְהֶבֶל הַיֹּפִי (sheqer hachen vehevel hayyofi)

a: A woman who fears the LORD
t: The book ends where it began
p: Proverbs opens with "the fear of the LORD" (1:7) and closes with a woman who fears the LORD.
b: The first lesson of the book is that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (1:7), and Wisdom repeats it at the end of her speeches (9:10). The last poem names its heroine's secret in the same words. So the book is framed by "the fear of the LORD": what was taught as a principle at the start is shown as a person at the end. Psalm 112, another acrostic, says, "Happy is the person who fears the LORD" (Psalm 112:1), and describes that person much as this poem describes her. The Greek changes the line (see the variant).

a: Give her a share of the fruit of her hands
p: The poem ends with a command to the whole community: let her have the reward of her work, and let it be praised in public.
b: The plural "give" (tenu) is addressed to the whole community. She has earned "the fruit of her hands" (compare 31:16), and her deeds should be praised "at the gates", where her husband sits (31:23). Jewish custom has used this poem at the end of a woman's life too: in Sephardi practice its first verse is recited before the memorial prayer at women's funerals, and lines from it are carved on tombstones. In many Jewish homes it is sung every Friday evening (see the chapter page).
